As of 302 PM EDT Tuesday...

KEY MESSAGE 1: Satellite imagery shows stratus eroding and becoming 
stratocumulus across much of northern New York and portions of 
central Vermont, especially southeast of the higher peaks
leading to only localized patches of blue sky this afternoon. A
sharper clearing line is still well to our north and west near 
the Ottawa Valley; these trends suggest skies will clear near
the International Border towards sunset. Overall, this setup
leads to a challenging sky cover forecast overnight. The 
clearing timing will delay fog formation, but think because 
dewpoint depressions are so small today, it won't take long for 
temperatures to pass their crossover values. As such, the 
thinking is mostly unchanged with regards quite a bit of fog to
develop especially after midnight, with relatively late timing 
in central/northeastern Vermont. However, continued light 
north- northwesterly flow may help maintain clouds and limit fog
in some areas that typically see fog, such as the Upper Valley 
in Vermont.

With mainly clear skies aside from aside from a large veil of
high clouds associated with a plume of deep moisture blowing off
from convection in the southwestern US, it will be a much milder
day on Wednesday. High temperatures expected to be a few to 
several degrees above normal, ranging from the upper 60s to mid 
70s. Aside from the localized stronger south winds on Lake
Champlain, winds will be rather light as the center of high 
pressure shifts to our southeast.

KEY MESSAGE 2: Sunshine will be more variable on Thursday as we
get under the influence of the first of a few waves of low
pressure extending from the closed upper level low that will
have been responsible for excessive rain across a swath of the
southwestern US into the central Plains states. The bulk of the
rain we see from this system is on track to come through on
Friday. However, most model guidance now shows some showers 
moving eastward through the Adirondacks and northern Vermont 
Thursday afternoon into the evening, likely driven by isentropic
lift in a moistening warm advection pattern. Have trended PoPs 
upward and added some spotty measurable rain amounts for this 
period, but with the air mass being a modified tropical one, the
environment will become favorable for efficient rainfall. 

No indications for particularly heavy rain were noted, but warm
rain processes will support downpours and locally higher 
rainfall amounts. This applies for both Thursday 
afternoon/evening and again Thursday night into Friday as a cold
front sharpens to our west and pushes through. The front still 
looks to cross relatively quickly during the Friday morning 
hours. As a result, there is a fairly large spread in possible 
temperatures on Friday given the impact of both cloud cover and 
cold air advection as the system pushes through. Generally we 
can expect a cooler day in our northern/western areas, while 
central and southern portions of Vermont may see temperatures 
just as warm as Thursday, reaching the mid or upper 70s.

KEY MESSAGE 3: The large scale pattern supports a mean mid/upper lvl 
trof developing across the Great Lakes into the NE CONUS for late 
weekend into next week, which wl produce below normal temps and 
mostly mtn precip chances. The highest probability of measurable 
precipitation wl be favorable nw upslope areas of the northern Dacks 
and central/northern Greens on Monday. The latest trends for Sunday 
precip shows an area going to our north, closer to the better 
forcing and another patch of precip sliding to our south. However, 
still thinking chc probability in the 30-40% range is reasonable 
from WPC this aftn. However, pops on Monday/Monday night probably 
need to be doubled from WPC, especially with a period of favorable 
upslope flow and strong llvl caa. The window is limited as flow 
aloft is progressive and the closed circulation is well north of our 
cwa, while best deep layer moisture is south and east of our fa. The 
big story going into next week wl be the window of much below normal 
temps with progged 850mb temps btwn -5C and -8C off the latest 12z 
GFS and sub-530 dam thickness values acrs our fa. Latest WPC 
guidance shows temps in the mid 50s to lower 60s on Monday and 
mostly 50s for Tues with lows 30 to 45F Monday night and 23F at SLK 
to upper 30s near Lake Champlain. Early guidance indicates this 
could be the coldest airmass of the fall season impacting our cwa 
early next week. However, as flow remains progressive with no deep 
amplification, warmer air redevelops by the middle of next week 
again.
